opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Geoff's influence is hard to overstate, even for people who never worked directly with him, because so much of the field's intuition comes from the line of thinking he championed for decades when it wasn't fashionable.

For me, the biggest thing I took from that brain-inspired view isn't the idea that we should copy biology neuron by neuron. It's the belief that intelligence comes from learning good representations from lots of data, rather than from hand-engineering rules or features. The brain doesn't come preloaded with a dictionary or a grammar textbook; it figures out structure by being exposed to the world. That framing pushed me toward questions like: how much can a model learn on its own, without labels, just by trying to predict or reconstruct what it sees?

That's really what drew me to work on pretraining for language. Some of the early work I did with Quoc Le on semi-supervised sequence learning was about taking a recurrent network, training it first as a language model or an autoencoder on unlabeled text, and then fine-tuning it on a downstream task. The intuition was very much in that tradition: let the network build up its own internal representation of language first, the way a person absorbs language long before anyone formally teaches them anything, and then specialize. At the time it wasn't obvious that would be the dominant paradigm, but it ended up being a core ingredient of where large language models went.

The other part of Geoff's taste that I really value is a kind of patience and conviction. He kept working on neural networks through periods when most people thought they were a dead end, and he was guided by intuition about what *should* work, given how brains seem to operate, even before the compute and data existed to prove it. That taught me that it's okay to pursue an idea that looks unfashionable if you have a principled reason to believe in it, and that scale can sometimes unlock things that looked hopeless at small sizes.

At the same time, I'd say I'm a bit more pragmatic about the brain analogy. It's a great source of inspiration and hypotheses, things like distributed representations, learning from prediction, maybe sparsity or memory, but ultimately I judge an idea by whether it works empirically and scales. So I'd describe my research taste as: brain-inspired in its ambitions, very empirical in its methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that Geoff's influence on me was less about any particular architecture and more about a way of asking questions. When I was at Google Brain, working around him and around people who had absorbed his habits, the thing that stuck was this insistence on starting from "how might the brain actually do this?" rather than "what's the cleanest mathematical formulation?" Those aren't the same question, and for a long time the field mostly rewarded the second one.

What that did to my taste is that I became suspicious of methods that work only because we've engineered them very carefully. If something requires a ton of hand-tuned supervision or a very specific loss function to get off the ground, my instinct now is that it's probably not the right abstraction. Brains learn from enormous amounts of unlabeled experience with very sparse feedback. So a lot of my work ended up gravitating toward semi-supervised and unsupervised learning, pretraining on raw sequences, things like that, because that's the regime that feels biologically plausible even if the exact mechanism isn't.

The other thing he modeled, which I think is underappreciated, is patience with ideas that look dumb. Neural nets were considered a dead end for a good chunk of his career, and he just kept going. That taught me that a reasonable prior is "if it resembles something the brain does, it probably deserves more attempts than the literature has given it." Capsules are a good example. Whether or not they pan out, the motivation behind them, that the visual system represents part-whole relationships explicitly, is a very Geoff kind of question, and I find that mode of thinking more generative than chasing whatever benchmark is hot that quarter.

So I'd say he didn't give me a toolkit. He gave me a bias toward asking what nature has already solved, and a tolerance for being wrong in public for a while before being right.

astra-6.text:
One thing I took from Jeff is the willingness to trust a simple idea and really explore it, even when it isn’t the fashionable direction. He uses intuition about how the brain might learn to ask questions that you might not arrive at just by looking at existing machine-learning techniques.

For me, that connects to an interest in learning from unlabeled data. Humans learn a tremendous amount just by observing the world; we don’t need someone to label every experience. So the question is: can we get a model to learn useful representations from the data itself, then use those representations for a particular task?

I wouldn’t say that means trying to copy the brain literally. It’s more about using it as a source of hypotheses, then testing whether those ideas actually work. That combination of ambitious intuition and empirical testing is what I find compelling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Jeff’s influence on me is less about copying the brain literally and more about taking learning seriously. Instead of hand-designing every piece of a system, you ask: can we set up a learning problem where useful representations emerge from the data?

That’s shaped my taste toward fairly general methods—approaches that can learn from lots of unlabeled data and then transfer what they’ve learned to different tasks. The brain is an inspiration, but ultimately you still have to run the experiment and see whether the idea works.
